title: Episode 10: Notifications and Mentions
description: Managing your notification inbox, @mentions, and strategies for avoiding overload.
concepts: How GitHub generates notifications: participating versus watching
Notification types: mention, review request, assignment, CI status
Marking notifications as read, done, or saved
Watch settings: watching, not watching, ignoring, custom
Using @mentions to get someone's attention in a comment
Strategies for managing notification volume without missing important items
Using gh CLI for notification-like workflows
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're talking about GitHub notifications, which sounds administrative, but it's really about protecting your attention.

[JAMIE]
I'm glad you said that, because notifications can feel like the moment GitHub stops being helpful and starts becoming noisy.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The goal is not to see everything. The goal is to notice the things that truly need you: a review request, an assignment, an @mention, maybe activity in a thread you're already part of.

[JAMIE]
So this is less about inbox perfection and more about building a workflow.

[ALEX]
Yes. A useful workflow, ideally one you can manage with just a keyboard and screen reader. And if you want a related reference later, there are also appendices on community and social features, discussions and gists, and the GitHub mobile app. For the core concepts today, GitHub's own documentation on notifications is the main authoritative source.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's start with the practical framing for this workshop. This part is guided practice, not a graded automation check.

[JAMIE]
Meaning there isn't a bot verifying your notification settings.

[ALEX]
Right. Notification settings are account-level, so the Learning Room pull request bot can't validate them. Instead, you'll do one guided walkthrough, then leave structured evidence in your assigned challenge issue.

[JAMIE]
What's the pattern learners should listen for?

[ALEX]
Configure, filter, act.

[JAMIE]
That is pleasingly compact.

[ALEX]
It's also realistic. First, configure your watch level so GitHub doesn't flood you. Second, filter your inbox so you can find the important items quickly. Third, act on what you find by responding, marking done, or muting.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Can you walk us through the actual challenge flow?

[ALEX]
Absolutely. The single challenge here is to configure notifications and practice inbox management.

First, open your Learning Room repository on GitHub.com.
Second, find the Watch button near the top right of the repository page, close to Star and Fork.
Third, open that Watch menu and choose Participating and @mentions.

[JAMIE]
And that setting means what, exactly?

[ALEX]
It means GitHub mainly notifies you when you are directly involved. If you comment on a thread, get assigned, or someone mentions your username, you'll hear about it. But you won't get every single issue and comment in the repository.

[JAMIE]
Which is probably the right choice for most learners.

[ALEX]
Very much so. After that, open the notifications inbox. You can go directly to github.com slash notifications, or use the bell icon in the GitHub header.

Then test two filters. Turn on Review requested, which shows notifications where someone asked you to review a pull request. Then clear that filter and turn on Assigned, which shows issues and pull requests assigned to you.

[JAMIE]
So we are practicing finding two common categories of work.

[ALEX]
Exactly. After that, open one notification by activating its title link, read it briefly, then go back to the inbox. Finally, perform one inbox action on a non-critical thread. You can mute it, or mark it done.

[JAMIE]
And the difference matters, right?

[ALEX]
It does. Mark done removes it from your current inbox, but you can still get future updates on that thread. Mute means you're saying, I do not want future updates from this thread.

[JAMIE]
That sounds like a good distinction to memorize.

[ALEX]
It is. And here's the simple screen reader framing: the notification list behaves like a standard list of links. Each item usually announces the title, the repository, and the reason, such as mention, review request, or assignment. Move through notifications with arrow keys, and press Enter to open one.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What counts as done for the challenge?

[ALEX]
Three things. You changed the watch level, you tested two different filters, and you performed one inbox action, either mute or mark done.

[JAMIE]
And then you need to submit evidence.

[ALEX]
Yes. In your assigned Chapter 10 challenge issue, post a completion comment with three details: your watch level, the filters you tested, and which inbox action you performed on which thread. Then close the challenge issue when you're done.

[JAMIE]
And the expected outcomes are pretty straightforward: reduce noise, find review and assigned work quickly, and clean up notifications intentionally.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get deeper, what if things don't line up the way the instructions suggest?

[ALEX]
Good question. If you can't find the Watch button, look near the top right of the repository page, in the same row as Star and Fork. If your notification inbox is empty, that's okay. You may simply not have any active notifications yet. You can switch to the Done tab and practice with an older item.

[JAMIE]
What if keyboard shortcuts don't work?

[ALEX]
Sometimes the screen reader intercepts the key. If that happens, click or focus the notification row first, then try again. Also, apply filters one at a time. If results seem strange, clear existing filters before adding a new one.

[JAMIE]
And if someone is still unsure?

[ALEX]
Ask a facilitator to model one inbox action live, then repeat it yourself. The point is to build confidence, not to guess silently.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now let's look at what actually generates a notification.

[JAMIE]
Because a lot of anxiety comes from not knowing why GitHub is talking to you.

[ALEX]
Exactly. GitHub may notify you when someone @mentions your username in an issue, pull request, or discussion. You may be notified when you're requested as a reviewer on a pull request. You may be notified when an issue or pull request is assigned to you.

[JAMIE]
Those all feel personal and direct.

[ALEX]
They are. You can also get notifications from threads you're subscribed to, maybe because you commented there, were mentioned there, or explicitly chose to subscribe. If a CI check fails on your pull request, GitHub Actions may generate a failure notification. And if you're watching a repository for all activity, even things like published releases can trigger notifications.

[JAMIE]
So there are really two big buckets: things involving me directly, and things I subscribed to broadly.

[ALEX]
That's a great mental model.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's unpack subscription levels, because this is where people often either miss important things or get buried.

[ALEX]
For each repository, you choose how much activity you want. Participating and @mentions gives you notifications only when you're part of the conversation or specifically addressed. That's the recommended setting for most repositories.

All Activity gives you essentially everything: issues opened, comments, pull requests, updates. Useful for your own repository, maybe, or for a situation where you truly need a broad pulse. But often it's too noisy.

Ignore means no notifications from that repository at all.

And Custom gives you finer control, such as issues only, pull requests only, releases, and similar options.

[JAMIE]
So the workshop recommendation is clear: Participating and @mentions for most repos.

[ALEX]
Yes. It keeps you in the loop without punishing you for joining a project.

[JAMIE]
How do you change it accessibly?

[ALEX]
On any repository page, find the Watch button in the header area. Mouse users can click it and choose from the dropdown. Screen reader users on Windows can jump through buttons, find Watch or Unwatch, press Enter, move up and down through the menu, and press Enter again to choose a level. On macOS with VoiceOver, use Quick Nav or VoiceOver navigation to the Watch button, open it with VO+Space, move through the choices, and select with VO+Space.

[JAMIE]
And the button label updates afterward?

[ALEX]
Yes, that change is your confirmation.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's go to the inbox itself.

[ALEX]
Your notifications inbox lives at github.com slash notifications. There's also a keyboard shortcut on GitHub: press G, then N.

[JAMIE]
Sequentially, not together.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Press G, release it, then press N. That matters, especially in browse mode with a screen reader.

[JAMIE]
What can you do once you're there?

[ALEX]
In the browser, the key actions include marking an item done, toggling read or unread, and muting a thread. The source material specifically calls out E to mark done, I to mark read or unread, and Shift+M to mute a thread.

[JAMIE]
Interesting, because the challenge directions mention M for mute.

[ALEX]
Right, and that's a useful teaching note: interface shortcuts can vary over time or by context, so if a key doesn't do what you expect, rely on focused controls in the page and the visible commands in the web interface. The important concepts are the actions themselves: done, read state, and mute.

[JAMIE]
What about outside the browser?

[ALEX]
In VS Code, if you use the GitHub Pull Requests extension, there's a Notifications view in the GitHub sidebar. You can open a related issue or pull request directly from there. GitHub Desktop does not manage notifications, so use the browser or command line instead.

[JAMIE]
And the command line options?

[ALEX]
GitHub CLI is useful for checking related work, even though it does not have a first-class dedicated notifications command for full inbox management.

For example, you can list pull requests requesting your review with a search command for review-requested at me. You can open the notifications page in your browser with gh browse notifications. You can also call the notifications API to inspect recent notification subjects, list issues assigned to you, or view a particular pull request if a notification references it.

[JAMIE]
So CLI is good for triage and context, but not the full mute-archive-manage experience.

[ALEX]
Exactly. For complete inbox management, the web interface is still the main tool.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's make the inbox concrete. What is the page structure like?

[ALEX]
Think of it as a page with navigation controls, filters, and then a list of notifications. Each notification row typically includes the title of the issue or pull request, the repository name, and a reason label telling you why it reached your inbox.

[JAMIE]
Like review requested, assigned, or mention.

[ALEX]
Exactly. That reason is often the quickest clue about urgency. A review request usually means someone is waiting on you. Assigned means you own follow-up. Mention means someone explicitly pulled you into a conversation.

[JAMIE]
How should a screen reader user move through the list?

[ALEX]
Usually as a list of links or interactive rows. Use arrow keys or normal reading navigation to move item by item. Listen for the title, repository, and reason. Open the title link with Enter when you want the full context. Then return to the inbox and continue.

[JAMIE]
And what gets announced per notification is important because it determines whether you can triage quickly.

[ALEX]
Exactly. You don't want to open every item just to know whether it matters.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What are the most useful inbox actions and shortcuts to remember?

[ALEX]
Conceptually, remember three things. First, mark done when you've processed something and want it out of your current inbox view. Second, mute when a thread is noisy and no longer relevant to you. Third, read or unread state can help you keep track of what still needs attention.

[JAMIE]
So this is really about making the inbox reflect reality.

[ALEX]
Yes. If everything stays in the inbox forever, the inbox stops meaning anything.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
How about filtering? Because that's often the difference between panic and clarity.

[ALEX]
Filtering is one of the most powerful habits here. You can filter by reason, like review requested or assigned. You can also filter by repository or organization.

[JAMIE]
That would help if you contribute to multiple places.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Instead of scanning a mixed stream of everything, you narrow the list to one repo, one org, or one kind of task. In practice, that means if you're sitting down to do review work, filter to review requests. If you're planning your own tasks, filter to assigned items. If you only want to think about one workshop repository, filter to that repository.

[JAMIE]
And if filters seem broken?

[ALEX]
Clear the active filters first, then apply one at a time. Stacking filters can be useful, but it can also hide results in ways that feel mysterious if you forget what's already active.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's talk about scale. Suppose the inbox is no longer tiny.

[ALEX]
Then you need deliberate habits. One important workflow is mark all as done.

[JAMIE]
That sounds a little dangerous.

[ALEX]
It can be, if used carelessly. But it's helpful when you've reviewed a batch of low-priority notifications and want to reset the inbox to only current, active work. The principle is not to preserve clutter for sentimental reasons.

[JAMIE]
And muting a noisy thread?

[ALEX]
Very useful. If a conversation keeps updating but no longer needs your involvement, mute it. That prevents future updates from continuing to consume your attention.

[JAMIE]
What about unexpected @mentions? Those can feel socially awkward.

[ALEX]
They can. Sometimes you're mentioned because someone thinks you can help. Sometimes they used your name broadly. The healthy response is to assess whether action is actually needed. If yes, respond or redirect. If no, and the thread keeps producing noise, mark it done or mute it. Being mentioned does not obligate you to live inside the thread forever.

[JAMIE]
That is a surprisingly freeing sentence.

[ALEX]
Good notification management at scale means not every ping becomes a commitment.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
The source also points to account-level notification settings. What should learners know there?

[ALEX]
Some notification preferences apply across your account, not just one repository. That can include delivery methods and broader subscription behavior. The key practical idea is that repository watch settings are only one layer. Your account settings also shape how and where notifications reach you.

[JAMIE]
So if someone says, I changed the repo watch level but I'm still getting more than expected, account settings might be part of the explanation.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
I definitely want to cover starring versus watching, because people mix those up constantly.

[ALEX]
They do. Starring a repository is mostly a bookmarking or appreciation signal. It says, I want to remember this repo, or I think it's interesting. Watching a repository affects notifications.

[JAMIE]
So star is social and organizational. Watch is operational.

[ALEX]
Perfectly said. If you star a repo, you are not necessarily signing up for updates. If you watch it, you are.

[JAMIE]
Let's do the two sides clearly. What does starring involve?

[ALEX]
Starring is a lightweight way to save or endorse a repository. It helps you find it later and can signal interest publicly.

[JAMIE]
And watching?

[ALEX]
Watching subscribes you to notifications according to the level you choose: participating only, all activity, custom, or ignore.

[JAMIE]
What's the common mistake?

[ALEX]
Accidental watching. Someone means to star a repo, or they click around the Watch controls without realizing they've subscribed to far more updates than they wanted.

[JAMIE]
How do they fix it?

[ALEX]
Go back to the repository's Watch menu and lower the subscription level. In many cases, set it to Participating and @mentions. If you truly want silence, choose Ignore.

[JAMIE]
And for this workshop, the recommendation stays the same.

[ALEX]
Yes. Use Participating and @mentions unless you have a specific reason to broaden it.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's give some screen reader-specific tips, because the inbox can be busy.

[ALEX]
For NVDA users, browse mode is often useful for reading the page structure and hearing the list of notifications, but you may need focus mode or direct interaction when using keyboard shortcuts on specific rows. If a shortcut seems swallowed, move focus deliberately to the notification item first.

[JAMIE]
And JAWS?

[ALEX]
Similar principle. Use quick navigation to move through links, buttons, and regions, and be aware that some single-letter keys may be intercepted by screen reader commands depending on mode. If GitHub shortcuts don't respond, switch interaction approach and focus the item directly.

[JAMIE]
What about VoiceOver on macOS?

[ALEX]
Use the rotor or normal web navigation to move through links, buttons, and lists. When working with menu buttons like Watch, VO+Space is your friend. In the inbox, listen for the reason label as part of each item so you can triage without opening everything.

[JAMIE]
So across all three screen readers, the strategy is: understand the page landmarks, focus the right control, and don't assume a shortcut failing means you did something wrong.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Sometimes it's just a mode issue.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
There's also a note about the GitHub mobile app.

[ALEX]
Yes. Think of mobile as a reference option, not the primary workflow for this lesson. You can manage notifications on your phone, but for learning the inbox structure, filters, and actions clearly, the browser is the best place to practice.

[JAMIE]
Especially when you're trying to understand watch settings and keyboard flows.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's turn this into a quick practical exercise. If someone wants to tame their inbox today, what should they actually do?

[ALEX]
Do a short routine.
Set your Learning Room repository to Participating and @mentions.
Open github.com slash notifications.
Filter to Review requested and see whether anything needs your attention.
Clear that and filter to Assigned.
Open one item.
Then choose one action on a non-critical thread: mark it done, or mute it.

[JAMIE]
That's small enough to repeat daily.

[ALEX]
And that is the point. Notification management works best as a light recurring habit, not a dramatic cleanup every three weeks.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
I want to end the day with a sense of progress. What did learners accomplish today, beyond just learning a new page?

[ALEX]
A lot, actually. You practiced controlling noise instead of just enduring it. You learned what kinds of events generate notifications. You learned the difference between broad subscriptions and direct involvement. You practiced finding review requests and assigned work. And you learned actions that keep your inbox meaningful.

[JAMIE]
If this was someone's first time managing GitHub notifications, that's a big shift.

[ALEX]
It is. And if this was your first time, remember: an empty inbox is not failure, and a noisy inbox is not a personal flaw. Both are normal states while learning. What matters is that you now know how to shape the system.

[JAMIE]
Let's do a quick confidence check.

[ALEX]
Ask yourself: can I explain what Participating and @mentions means? Can I find review requests? Can I find assigned issues or pull requests? Do I know when to use mark done versus mute? If yes, you're on solid ground.

[JAMIE]
And your challenge progress for this chapter is simply whether you completed the walkthrough and posted the evidence comment.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
So what happens next, after today?

[ALEX]
Day 2 builds on this foundation. The more comfortable you are with notifications, the easier it is to stay responsive during collaboration. Between days, a good habit is to check filtered notifications once or twice a day rather than constantly.

[JAMIE]
That feels healthier than living inside the bell menu.

[ALEX]
Much healthier. And one final encouragement: you already know more than you think. If you can set a watch level, filter for review requests, and decide whether to mark something done or mute it, you are already practicing a real open source contribution skill.

[JAMIE]
Not glamorous, but deeply practical.

[ALEX]
And practical is powerful. Good contributors are not the people who read every notification. They're the people who know how to notice the right things.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we close, can you restate the core learning pattern one more time?

[ALEX]
Gladly. Configure settings proactively before the noise starts. Use filters to find signal in the noise. Take a clear action on each notification: respond, mark done, or mute. Then build a daily routine that keeps the inbox manageable.

[JAMIE]
That's the whole lesson in four moves.

[ALEX]
It is. And with that, you've finished today's work: set your notification flow, submit your completion comment on the assigned challenge issue, and close that issue when done.

[JAMIE]
Nice work, everyone.

[ALEX]
See you next time.

# Notifications
>
> **Listen to Episode 10:** [Notifications and Mentions](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Related appendices:** [Appendix T: Community and Social](appendix-t-community-and-social.md) | [Appendix U: Discussions and Gists](appendix-u-discussions-and-gists.md) | [Appendix V: GitHub Mobile](appendix-v-github-mobile.md)
> **Authoritative sources:** [GitHub Docs: About notifications](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/managing-subscriptions-and-notifications-on-github/setting-up-notifications/about-notifications)

## Managing Your GitHub Notification Inbox

> **See also:** [Appendix V: GitHub Mobile](appendix-v-github-mobile.md) for managing notifications on your phone.

> GitHub notifications are how GitHub tells you when something needs your attention. This guide teaches you to keep the inbox useful - not overwhelming - using only your keyboard and screen reader.

## Workshop Recommendation (Chapter 10)

For this workshop, Chapter 10 is a **guided practice chapter**, not a graded automation chapter.

- **Challenge count:** 1 guided walkthrough
- **Automation check:** none - notification settings are account-level and cannot be validated by the Learning Room PR bot
- **Evidence:** structured completion comment on your assigned challenge issue
- **Pattern:** configure, filter, act

### Important Note: This Challenge Uses GitHub's Web Notification Inbox

This challenge focuses on **GitHub's web-based notification inbox** (at `github.com/notifications`), not email notifications. You do NOT need to configure email delivery, and you do NOT need to receive emails to complete this challenge.

**Why we focus on the web inbox:**

- Email delivery depends on your mail server, ISP, spam filters, and account settings—factors outside our control
- GitHub's web notification inbox is always available and works the same way for everyone
- Professional developers typically check notifications in the GitHub app or web UI rather than waiting for emails
- The skills you learn (filtering, muting, managing noise) apply whether you eventually enable email or not

**What you will do:**

- Use GitHub's web notification inbox to view and filter notifications
- Configure repository watch levels to control what notifications you receive
- Practice managing your inbox with GitHub's built-in actions (mute, mark done)

If you have already configured email notifications on your GitHub account, that is fine—but this challenge does not require or test email delivery. Focus on the web inbox workflow instead.

### Chapter 10 Challenge Set

1. **Configure notifications and practice inbox management** - set your watch level, use filters to find relevant notifications, and perform one inbox action.

### Challenge 10.1 Step-by-Step: Notification Inbox Walkthrough

**Goal:** Set up a useful notification workflow so you can keep up with reviews, mentions, and assignments without inbox overload.

**Where you are working:** the GitHub.com notifications page and your Learning Room repository settings.

**Estimated time:** 5-8 minutes.

1. Open your Learning Room repository on GitHub.com.
2. Find the **Watch** button near the top-right of the repository page (next to Star and Fork).
3. Activate the **Watch** dropdown and select **Participating and @mentions**. This means you only get notified when someone @mentions you or you are directly participating in a thread.
4. Open the notifications inbox by navigating to `https://github.com/notifications` (or activate the bell icon in the GitHub header).
5. In the notification filters, activate the **Review requested** filter. This shows only notifications where someone has asked you to review their PR.
6. Clear that filter and activate the **Assigned** filter. This shows notifications for issues and PRs assigned to you.
7. Open one notification by activating its title link. Read it briefly, then navigate back to the inbox.
8. Perform one inbox action on a non-critical notification thread:
   - Press `M` to **mute** the thread (you will not receive future updates), or
   - Press `E` to **mark done** (removes it from inbox but you can still get future updates).

**Screen reader tip:** The notification list is a standard list of links. Each notification announces its title, repository, and reason (mention, review request, assignment). Use arrow keys to move between notifications and `Enter` to open one.

**You are done when:** You have changed your watch level, used two different filters, and performed one inbox action (mute or done).

### Completing Chapter 10: Submit Your Evidence

Open your **assigned Chapter 10 challenge issue** and post a completion comment:

```text
Chapter 10 completed:
- Watch level set to: Participating and @mentions
- Filters tested: Review requested, Assigned
- Inbox action performed: [mute / mark done] on [thread description]
```

Close your Chapter 10 challenge issue when done.

### Expected Outcomes

- Student can configure repository watch levels to reduce noise.
- Student can find review requests and assigned work quickly using filters.
- Student can reduce notification noise with mute or done actions.

### If You Get Stuck

1. Can't find the Watch button? It is near the top-right of the repository page, in the same row as Star and Fork.
2. Notification inbox is empty? You may not have any notifications yet - that is fine. Switch to the **Done** tab and practice the mute/done action flow on an older notification.
3. Keyboard shortcuts not working? If your screen reader intercepts `M` or `E`, click on the notification row first to give it focus, then press the shortcut.
4. Filters not showing results? Clear all filters first (click the X next to each active filter), then apply one filter at a time.
5. Ask facilitator to model one inbox action live, then repeat the steps yourself.
6. Finished but not sure you did it right? Compare your work against the [Challenge 9 reference solution](solutions/solution-09-merge-day.md).

### Learning Moment

Notification management protects focus. You can stay responsive to your team without drowning in updates. The habit you build here - checking filtered notifications once or twice a day - is how productive open source contributors stay on top of their work.

### Learning Pattern Used in This Chapter

1. Configure settings proactively (watch level) before work generates noise.
2. Use filters to find signal in noise (review requests, assignments).
3. Take decisive action on each notification (mute, done, or respond).
4. Build a daily routine that keeps your inbox manageable.

## What Generates a Notification?

GitHub sends you a notification when:

| Event | You are notified if... |
| -------  | ------------------------  |
| Someone @mentions you | `@your-username` appears in any issue, PR, or discussion |
| A PR is assigned to you for review | You are added as a reviewer |
| An issue or PR is assigned to you | You are assigned |
| There is activity on a thread you are subscribed to | You commented, were mentioned, or chose to subscribe |
| A CI check fails on your PR | Actions sends a failure notification |
| A release is published | You are watching the repo for all activity |

## Notification Subscription Levels

For each repository, you choose how many notifications to receive:

| Level | What You Receive |
| -------  | -----------------  |
| **Participating and @mentions** | Only notifications where you participated (commented, were assigned, @mentioned). Recommended for most repos. |
| **All Activity** | Every issue opened, every comment, every PR. Only use this for your own repos or very active contribution. |
| **Ignore** | No notifications from this repo at all. |
| **Custom** | Fine-grained control: issues only, PRs only, releases, etc. |

### Changing your watch settings for a repo

<details>
<summary>Visual / mouse users</summary>

At the top of any repository page, find the **Watch** button (near Star and Fork). Click it to open a dropdown with levels: **Participating and @mentions**, **All Activity**, **Custom**, and **Ignore**. Click your preferred level - it takes effect immediately.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users (NVDA / JAWS - Windows)</summary>

1. Find the **Watch** button in the repo header (`B` to navigate buttons → find "Watch [N]" or "Unwatch" button)
2. Press `Enter` to open the dropdown
3. Press `↑/↓` to navigate the subscription options
4. Press `Enter` to select your preferred level
5. The button label updates to confirm your choice

</details>

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users (VoiceOver - macOS)</summary>

1. Quick Nav `B` to find the **Watch** button in the repo header (listen for "Watch" or "Unwatch")
2. `VO+Space` to open the dropdown
3. `VO+Down` or arrow keys to navigate subscription options
4. `VO+Space` to select your preferred level
5. The button label updates to confirm your choice

</details>

**Recommended setting for most repos:** “Participating and @mentions only” - you stay in the loop on what involves you without noise.

## The Notifications Inbox

### Tool Cards: Manage Notifications

**github.com (browser):**

1. Go to [github.com/notifications](https://github.com/notifications) (or press `G` then `N`).
2. Use `E` to mark done, `I` to mark read/unread, `Shift+M` to mute a thread.

**VS Code Desktop (GitHub Pull Requests extension):**

1. The **Notifications** view in the GitHub sidebar shows items needing attention.
2. Click a notification to open the related issue or PR directly in VS Code.

**GitHub Desktop:**
GitHub Desktop does not manage notifications. Use the browser or CLI.

**Git CLI / GitHub CLI:**

```bash
# List PRs requesting your review (most common notification)
gh search prs --review-requested @me --state open
# Open the notifications page in your browser
gh browse notifications
```

Navigate to your inbox: `https://github.com/notifications` or press `G` then `N` (GitHub keyboard shortcut).

**Screen reader note:** The `G N` shortcut uses two sequential key presses (not simultaneous). Press `G`, release it, then press `N`. This works in Browse Mode.

<details>
<summary>GitHub CLI (gh) alternative - notifications</summary>

View and manage your GitHub notification status from the terminal:

```bash
# Check your notification status (opens the GitHub notification inbox)
gh api notifications --jq '.[].subject.title' | head -20

# View PRs that need your review (most common notification reason)
gh search prs --review-requested @me --state open

# View issues assigned to you
gh issue list --assignee @me --state open

# Check PR status for a specific notification
gh pr view 42 --repo owner/repo
```

**Note:** The GitHub CLI does not have a first-class `gh notifications` command. For full inbox management (mark as read, mute, archive), use the web interface at `github.com/notifications`. The `gh` CLI is most useful for quickly checking PR review requests and issue assignments that generate notifications.

</details>

## Starring vs. Watching - What Is the Difference?

New contributors often confuse these two. They appear next to each other on every repository page and do completely different things.

### Starring a Repository

| Feature | Description |
| ---  | ---  |
| **What it does** | Bookmarks the repository to your Stars list at `github.com/stars` |
| **Notifications** | **None.** Starring never sends you any notifications |
| **Visibility** | Public - anyone can see what you've starred on your profile |
| **Use case** | "I want to save this for later" or "I want to show appreciation" |
| **Keyboard path** | On any repo page: `B` to navigate buttons → find "Star" button → Enter |

Starring is GitHub's equivalent of a bookmark + public endorsement. The star count on a repository is a community signal of popularity. Many maintainers watch their star count as a rough measure of interest.

### Watching a Repository

| Feature | Description |
| ---  | ---  |
| **What it does** | Subscribes you to notifications from that repository |
| **Notifications** | Sends notifications based on your chosen level (see below) |
| **Visibility** | Private - other users cannot see what you're watching |
| **Use case** | "I need to stay informed about activity in this repo" |
| **Keyboard path** | `B` → find "Watch" button → Enter → ↑/↓ to pick a level → Enter |

### Common Mistake: Accidental Watching

When you comment on an issue or PR in a repository, GitHub **automatically subscribes you** to that thread - but not the whole repository. However, if you once click "Watch" on a busy repository (say, a popular open source project), you will receive a notification for every issue opened and every comment posted - potentially hundreds per day.

#### How to silence a repository you accidentally over-subscribed to

```text
Step 1: Navigate to the repository
Step 2: B → Find "Unwatch" button → Enter
Step 3: Select "Participating and @mentions"
Step 4: Enter to confirm
```

This immediately reduces notifications from that repository to only threads you personally participated in.

### Recommended Watching Strategy for This Workshop

| Repository | Recommended Watch Level |
| ---  | ---  |
| `community-access/accessibility-agents` | **Participating and @mentions** - you contribute there, you only need to hear back when someone replies to you |
| Your own fork | **All Activity** - this is your fork; know everything |
| Very busy popular repos | **Ignore** or **Participating** - do not watch for All Activity |
| Repos you're evaluating | **Star only** - save without subscribing |

## Try It: Tame Your Inbox

**Time:** 2 minutes | **What you need:** Browser, signed in to GitHub

Go to [github.com/notifications](https://github.com/notifications) and practice:

1. **Scan your inbox** - Press `H` and `Tab` to navigate through notifications. Each one shows the repo name, type (issue/PR), and title.
2. **Mark one as done** - Find a notification you've already read. Press `E` to mark it as done. It disappears from the list.
3. **Configure watching** - Go to the Learning Room repository. Press `D` to landmarks, find the repo nav area, then look for the "Watch" or "Unwatch" button (`B` to scan buttons). Choose your preferred watch level.

**You're done.** You now control what GitHub tells you about and what it doesn't.

> **What success feels like:** Your inbox has fewer items, and you chose what to watch. Notifications work *for* you now, not against you.

> ### Day 2 Amplifier - Accessibility Agents: `@daily-briefing`
>
> **Manage your notification inbox manually before using any agent.** The signal-versus-noise judgment you develop - what to act on, what to watch, what to mute - is the same judgment the agent applies when prioritizing its output. Without that judgment, you cannot evaluate whether the agent's prioritization is correct or whether it surfaced the things that actually matter to you.
>
> Once you have mastered manual notification management:
>
> - **In VS Code** - `@daily-briefing morning briefing` delivers the same information as your notification inbox, organized by priority and actionability, with the ability to reply, close, and merge from inside Copilot Chat
> - **In your repo** - Fork [accessibility-agents](https://github.com/Community-Access/accessibility-agents) and every collaborator on your project can run `@daily-briefing` against your shared repository; the whole team stays aligned from a single command with no inbox required
> - **In the cloud** - GitHub Agentic Workflows can run on a schedule and post a team digest to a designated issue each morning, surfacing what needs attention before anyone opens their notifications
>
> *Your notification discipline today becomes the standard the agent enforces at scale tomorrow.*

currentFacts: The Accessibility Agents collection grows over time. Refer to it as a living catalog rather than asserting a fixed count of agents.
Challenge 15 (Discover Accessibility Agents) is browse-first. Learners are not required to fork the accessibility-agents repository to complete it.
Completing Challenge 15 unlocks Challenge 16 (Capstone Project) plus Bonus Challenges A through E. The bonus challenges are a structured unlock path, not "things to do if you finish early".

Challenge 16 is titled "Capstone Project". It accepts contributions to Accessibility Agents, GLOW, or any other meaningful repository. Review-ready drafts and contribution plans are valid evidence of completion.
The Learning Room repository is where Day 1 contributions happen (issue, branch, commit, pull request, merge). It is provisioned per learner.
Hosts are Alex (warm expert) and Jamie (curious co-host who asks the questions learners hesitate to ask). They are colleagues, not teacher and student.
voiceRules.voiceExemplar:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're working with one of those GitHub features that quietly makes open source collaboration much easier: issue templates.

[JAMIE]
And this is a great one for people who have ever opened a blank issue form and thought, what exactly am I supposed to put here?

[ALEX]
Exactly. An issue template turns that blank box into a guided experience. Instead of guessing what maintainers need, contributors get prompts, structure, and clear required fields. That reduces back-and-forth, improves quality, and helps teams act on issues faster.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

[ALEX]
Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get into the design challenge, what should learners already have in place?

[ALEX]
A few practical things. First, you should already know how to work with GitHub issues at a basic level. Second, you need a repository where you can create or edit files, usually your fork or your own repo. Third, it really helps to use an editor with YAML syntax highlighting, such as VS Code.

[JAMIE]
And some things are recommended but not strictly required, right?

[ALEX]
Right. Familiarity with GitHub Copilot can help if you want to generate variations, but it's optional. Basic terminal comfort is useful, though you can also use the GitHub web editor or github.dev. And if you already filled out the workshop registration template earlier in this course, that template becomes a learning example now.

[JAMIE]
I like that. You've already used a professional issue template, so now you reverse-engineer it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Also, there's an administrative note here: this chapter is meant to prepare you for a later workflow using a template-building agent. The advice is to complete the manual template chapter first, then use the automation later.

[JAMIE]
And time-wise?

[ALEX]
Plan roughly two to two and a half hours if you do the exercises and some YAML troubleshooting.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The learning pattern for this challenge is analyze, remix, create, and test.

[JAMIE]
That feels approachable. First understand an existing template, then adapt one, then optionally build another version from scratch, then verify it works.

[ALEX]
That's the idea. The workshop recommendation frames Challenge 14 as design-focused rather than automation-focused. You're producing evidence of understanding, often as an issue comment or a pull request, rather than trying to satisfy a complicated code runtime.

[JAMIE]
Though there is still one small autograded requirement in the challenge template itself.

[ALEX]
Yes. For the assigned challenge issue, the autograder checks that a YAML file exists in the repository
